tier_reason: docs/benchmark.md compares rv32emu (tiered JIT) with QEMU v9.0.0 on an Intel Core i7-11700 with GCC 14.2.0 guest builds, but the speedups exist only in the jit-bench.png chart, the script that produced it is not named, and the host build flags of rv32emu and QEMU are not stated, so first-party with partial methodology. The VMIL'24 paper (abstract snippet only: 12%/35% overhead versus native x86/ARM, better than RV8 or QEMU) could not be opened; a paper-access retier could raise this to B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/benchmark.md says rv32emu with tiered JIT 'outperforms QEMU v9.0.0 across all benchmarks'; the speedup appears only in a normalised bar chart (docs/jit-bench.png, reciprocal of mean elapsed time over 200 iterations, QEMU = 1.0), read by eye (chart image, not stated in text): numeric sort about 2.07x, string sort about 2.6x, bitfield about 2.04x, emfloat about 1.5x, assignment about 2.85x, idea about 2.5x, huffman about 2.37x, dhrystone about 2.65x, primes about 1.25x, sha512 about 1.26x. Reference table on the same page (no QEMU column): Threadripper 2990WX Dhrystone 33,365 DMIPS (T2C) vs 2,533 (interpreter), about 13x (derived from page data); CoreMark 13,272 vs 1,835 iterations/s, about 7.2x (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Numbers for the QEMU comparison exist only in a PNG chart, values here are eyeballed. The page text calls primes, sha512 and emfloat the biggest gains while the chart shows them as the three smallest, so prose and chart disagree. QEMU flags, the rv32emu host build flags, which tiers were enabled (T1C only or T1C plus LLVM-based T2C) and the script that produced the chart are not named on the page (tests/interpreter_bench.py is for the libriscv comparison, tests/bench.py has no QEMU mode). The default build has since moved to T1C (defconfig), so the chart may not reflect the current default. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot. The peer-reviewed VMIL'24 paper (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3689490.3690399) is blocked here; its abstract (search snippet only) reports 12%/35% overhead versus native x86/ARM code and says the result beats RV8 and QEMU.

notes: Chart values match the record's 1.25x-2.85x range; record kept at C. Shortcomings: QEMU numbers chart-only, prose-chart contradiction on which benchmarks gain most, no named QEMU-comparison script or host flags, tier configuration of the charted run unstated. Metadata checked: MIT, 594 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-10-03.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: the peer-reviewed CARRV 2017 paper (opened via its raw.githubusercontent.com mirror of carrv.github.io) has runtime tables (Figures 7-10) for rv8 versus QEMU riscv64 and QEMU aarch64 on seven benchmarks, and the benchmark code is public in michaeljclark/rv8-bench. Not A: the paper states no host CPU, compiler or QEMU version; CPU (Core i7-5557U) and compiler (GCC 7.2.0, -O3/-O2/-Os, -fPIE) appear only in rv8-bench data/template.md, the template for the rv8.io/bench results page the paper cites, which later added a bigint benchmark, so its tie to the paper's run is unconfirmed.

corrections.claimed_speedup: CARRV 2017 paper (Clark and Hoult), Figure 9: geomean runtime ratio to native x86-64 at -O3 is rv8 2.62 vs QEMU riscv64 4.68 and QEMU aarch64 4.57, so about 1.79x faster than QEMU riscv64 and 1.74x faster than the faster QEMU (derived from page data); Figure 10 at -Os: rv8 2.47 vs QEMU riscv64 4.62 (about 1.87x, derived from page data) and QEMU aarch64 5.20. Conclusion: 'on average approximately 75% faster than the leading competitor', and on some benchmarks 'approximately 30% slower than native x86-64 code'. Per-benchmark -O3 runtimes (Figure 7, seconds, rv8 vs QEMU riscv64): qsort 1.22 vs 4.76, dhrystone 0.20 vs 0.57, primes 0.70 vs 1.26, aes 1.53 vs 2.16, miniz 1.60 vs 2.21, sha512 0.81 vs 1.24, norx 1.20 vs 1.17 (rv8 slower on norx).
corrections.workload: rv8-bench suite (aes, dhrystone, miniz, norx, primes, qsort, sha512) compiled for riscv64 at -O3 and -Os and run under the rv8 x86-64 JIT (hybrid interpretation plus translation of hot paths, macro-op fusion) and QEMU riscv64 user-mode, with QEMU aarch64 running aarch64 builds and native x86-64 builds as references; runtimes in seconds.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper states none. rv8-bench data/template.md: guest and native benchmarks built with GCC 7.2.0 and musl libc at -O3, -O2 and -Os, all -fPIE (its prose says GCC 7.1.0; README names musl-riscv-toolchain 7.1.0-2); best of 20 runs. Host build flags of rv8 and QEMU, and the QEMU version (riscv/riscv-qemu fork, 2017), not stated.
corrections.hardware: Paper names no CPU. rv8-bench data/template.md: Intel Core i7-5557U Broadwell, 3.10-3.40 GHz (the template calls it 6th-gen; the i7-5557U is a Broadwell part).
corrections.caveats: Paper is peer-reviewed but written by the project's authors; its summary table swaps the two QEMU columns relative to Figures 9 and 10 (the figures are internally consistent with the runtime tables). rv8 is slower than QEMU riscv64 on norx at -O3. The 'leading competitor' in the 75% claim is QEMU aarch64 running aarch64 binaries, not a RISC-V baseline. The paper omits CPU, compiler and QEMU version; those come from the rv8-bench results template, which may postdate the paper's run (rv8.io/bench, the cited results page, was not reachable). Repo last touched 2018 and now lives at larkmjc/rv8 (the michaeljclark URL redirects). Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot. rv32emu's VMIL'24 abstract (snippet only) claims to beat rv8.

notes: Paper reached through raw.githubusercontent.com/carrv/carrv.github.io; numbers in the record's snippet are confirmed and now have tables, so tier raised C to B (could be A if rv8.io/bench shows the same numbers with the i7-5557U host). Shortcomings: paper omits CPU/compiler/QEMU version, swapped QEMU columns in its summary table, slower than QEMU on norx -O3, abandoned since 2018. Metadata checked: MIT (LICENSE lacks a copyright line), 727 stars, last commit 2018-09-22; GitHub now shows owner larkmjc.

tier_reason: The repo page has no numbers (record's D was right for that page), but the peer-reviewed OOPSLA 2014 paper 'The HipHop Virtual Machine' by Meta engineers reports, per search snippets of its abstract and ACM PDF, a 1.6x speedup over PHP on real-world applications in sandbox mode; the paper (dl.acm.org) is blocked, so snippet-only numbers cap this at C. A paper-access retier could raise it to B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (OOPSLA 2014 paper 'The HipHop Virtual Machine', Adams et al., not opened): 'in sandbox mode HHVM attains a 1.6x speedup over PHP when running real-world applications' (HPHPc could not run these applications; HHVM could not run Drupal); on the paper's benchmark suite HHVM reaches a geometric mean speedup of 2.64x in sandbox mode and 2.79x in production mode, compared to HPHPc's 1.93x (the snippet does not name the base of these ratios). The README itself only says HHVM 'uses a just-in-time (JIT) compilation approach to achieve superior performance'.
corrections.baseline: PHP reference interpreter (Zend Engine), 2014-era version per the OOPSLA 2014 paper (version not seen); HPHPc as a second comparison
corrections.caveats: Numbers are from search snippets of the OOPSLA 2014 paper (dl.acm.org and the SPLASH page are blocked here); PHP version, hardware and flags unverified. The comparison is against 2014-era PHP; PHP 7 and later changed the interpreter substantially, and the current README describes HHVM as a VM for programs written in Hack, so a Zend-PHP baseline no longer matches what current HHVM runs. Authors are Meta engineers (first-party, peer-reviewed). The Zend-2.0 licence part is not OSI-approved, hence usability mixed. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.

notes: Kept and raised D to C on paper-snippet numbers (1.6x over PHP on real-world apps, sandbox mode); paper not opened. Shortcomings: README has no numbers, evidence is a 2014 paper against PHP 5-era Zend, current HHVM runs Hack only per its README, Zend-2.0 licence non-OSI. Metadata checked: 18.7k stars, PHP-3.01 and Zend-2.0 core plus MIT Hack typechecker and HSL, last commit 2026-10-06.
